content: The elimination of kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis) as a public health problem is being pursued through a series of targeted strategies and milestones, supported by robust mathematical modeling and evidence-based interventions. Below are the detailed steps and actions planned for the elimination of kala-azar in the South-East Asia Region, as outlined by the World Health Organization (WHO): 1. Role of Asymptomatic Infections and Non-Human Reservoirs: Asymptomatic infections play a critical role in the transmission dynamics of Leishmania donovani. Understanding their contribution is essential for designing effective control measures. Non-human reservoirs may also contribute to the persistence of transmission in endemic areas, necessitating further research and targeted interventions. 2. Key Milestones by 2023: A high-level ministerial meeting will be convened among endemic countries at the regional level to renew the memorandum of understanding (MoU) for collaboration on kala-azar elimination. WHO will develop and disseminate standard indicators to monitor the performance of surveillance systems for kala-azar and post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL). A training package for skin-related neglected tropical diseases (NTDs), including PKDL, will be developed and disseminated for use in primary health care settings. WHO will also create and distribute an integrated vector management training package. A mechanism for cross-border surveillance and notification of kala-azar and PKDL cases will be established in collaboration with relevant Member States. At least one endemic country will be validated by WHO as having achieved the elimination of kala-azar as a public health problem. 3. Key Milestones by 2024: All endemic countries in the region will strengthen national notification systems for kala-azar and PKDL. Screening for kala-azar will be mandated for all HIV patients living in endemic areas, and vice versa, HIV screening will be required for all kala-azar patients. Follow-up and clinical reassessment of all kala-azar patients will be operationalized for at least three years post-treatment. Mechanisms will be established to ensure timely case reporting and referral of suspected kala-azar and PKDL cases from all health facilities, including private sector clinics, dermatologists, and informal healthcare providers, through integrated primary health care and strengthened health systems. 4. Key Milestones by 2025: WHO will update and disseminate guidance on treatment options for relapse cases of kala-azar. Endemic countries will determine feasible options for integrating kala-azar and PKDL surveillance with other diseases or platforms. Integrated vector surveillance and control measures, including those targeting kala-azar, will be operationalized in all endemic countries. 5. Key Milestones by 2026: All endemic implementation units in the region will achieve the targets for eliminating kala-azar as a public health problem. The progress and impacts of the Regional Strategic Framework will be assessed and updated as necessary. 6. Measuring Progress and Impacts: National kala-azar elimination programs will establish milestones for implementing strategic priorities as per the Regional Strategic Framework. These milestones will be evaluated regularly to ensure compliance with the targets and objectives. The implementation progress of the Regional Strategic Framework will be monitored at the regional level and guided by the Regional Technical Advisory Group (RTAG). 7. Treatment Regimens for Kala-Azar and PKDL: Preferred treatment regimens include liposomal amphotericin B, either as a single dose or over multiple days, and combination therapies with miltefosine or paromomycin. Rescue treatments for non-responsive cases include higher doses of liposomal amphotericin B or conventional amphotericin B deoxycholate infusions. For PKDL, treatment options include amphotericin B deoxycholate or miltefosine administered over extended periods. 8. Cross-Border Collaboration: WHO has facilitated meetings to strengthen cross-border collaboration for kala-azar elimination along the international borders of India with Bangladesh, Bhutan, and Nepal. Action points include signing cross-border collaboration MoUs, defining clear roles and responsibilities, and enhancing surveillance and notification systems. 9. Research and Evidence-Based Interventions: Studies have highlighted the changing clinico-epidemiology of PKDL, the role of biomarkers, and the use of xenodiagnosis to address key questions in kala-azar control. Advances in molecular diagnostics and real-time PCR have improved the detection of PKDL in endemic areas. Research on risk factors for relapse and the long-term incidence of PKDL has informed treatment strategies. 10. Sustainability and Post-Elimination Surveillance: Sustainable surveillance systems for neglected tropical diseases, including kala-azar, are critical for the post-elimination era. WHO has emphasized the integration of surveillance and control measures into broader health systems to ensure long-term sustainability. These efforts represent a comprehensive and multi-faceted approach to achieving and sustaining the elimination of kala-azar in the South-East Asia Region.
